title: X86ASM 21: The Heap and the brk System Call

questions.q: What is the main limitation of the data segment that makes a heap useful?
choices: It can't grow or shrink at runtime
Only the function that declared a variable can access it
Its contents are lost when the declaring function returns
It can only hold one byte per label
questions.explain: The data segment is global, so every function can access it, but its size is fixed. It can't be resized at runtime.

questions.q: Function A reserves space on the stack, then calls B, which calls C. What goes wrong if that memory needs to outlive A?
choices: B and C can't see A's stack memory at all
Once A returns, the memory is effectively gone, and accessing it is unreliable
The stack can't grow, so A can't reserve the space in the first place
The kernel zeroes the stack every time a function is called
questions.explain: The stack can grow and shrink, but space reserved there belongs to the function that reserved it. Functions A calls can use it while A is still running, but after A returns, using it is unreliable.

questions.q: If function A reserves stack space and then calls B, which calls C, then C can still use A's memory as long as A hasn't returned.
questions.explain: Every function A calls can see A's stack memory while A is still active. The problem only starts after A returns.

questions.q: Which of these describe heap memory allocated with brk?
choices: Any function in the program can use it
It stays valid after the function that allocated it returns
Its size can be changed at runtime
It's freed automatically when the allocating function returns
It's the modern way to allocate memory and can be placed almost anywhere in the address space
questions.explain: brk extends the data segment, so the heap is global and can grow at runtime. It stays valid until the program gives it back or exits. The modern approach, which can place memory in many different areas, is mmap, not brk.

questions.q: What is the 'program break'?
choices: The address of the first instruction in the text segment
The current top of the stack
The end of the data segment, where it meets unmapped memory
The address the program jumps to when it exits
questions.explain: The program break marks the end of the data segment. brk moves it to make that segment bigger or smaller.

questions.q: What is the system call number for brk on x86-64 Linux?
questions.explain: Before calling syscall, you put 12 in RAX.

questions.q: With RAX = 12 and RDI = 0, what does syscall return in RAX?
choices: An error, because 0 isn't a valid address
The current program break, which is where a new heap would start
The amount of free heap space in bytes
The address of the stack pointer
questions.explain: Calling brk with 0 asks the kernel where the program break is right now. Nothing has been allocated yet, so that address is where the heap will start.

questions.q: When you call brk to move the program break, which register holds the requested new break address?
choices: RAX
RDI
RSI
RSP
questions.explain: RDI holds the first syscall argument. RAX holds the syscall number (12) going in and the return value coming out.

questions.q: When a program starts and no heap has been allocated yet, the current program break is both the start and the end of the heap.
questions.explain: The heap is added onto the end of the data segment. Before anything is allocated it has zero size, so its start and end are the same address: the current break.

questions.q: You request a new program break with brk. How can you tell the kernel honored the request?
choices: RAX is 0 after the syscall
RAX holds the new break you asked for
RDI is set to -1
The program gets a SIGCHLD signal
questions.explain: In the example, the request for 0x402400 returned 0x402400 in RAX, which showed the space had been reserved.

questions.q: In some environment, a brk syscall returns -38 (and the program uses it as its exit code). What does that mean?
choices: Permission denied
Out of memory
Function not implemented (ENOSYS): the environment doesn't support that syscall
The requested address isn't page-aligned
questions.explain: Error number 38 is ENOSYS, 'function not implemented'. The emulated environment didn't support brk, so the program had to run on a real Linux system.

questions.q: Which system call does the lesson name as the modern alternative to brk for allocating memory?
questions.explain: brk is the classic way: it just extends the data segment. mmap is the modern way and can place memory in many different areas.

questions.q: brk(0) returns 0x402000. You add 1024 to it and call brk with the result. What should brk return if it succeeds? (Answer in hex.)
After allocation, the heap runs from 0x403000 to 0x403400. How many bytes is that, in decimal?
questions.explain: 0x403400 - 0x403000 = 0x400 = 1024 bytes. The video loosely calls this 'a thousand'.

questions.q: The program's instructions are at 0x401000 and 0x401007, and brk(0) returns 0x402000 (the program has no data). What does 0x402000 represent?
choices: The top of the stack
The end of the program image, where the mapped address space currently ends
The first byte of the text segment
An address chosen at random by the kernel on every run
questions.explain: 0x402000 is the end of the program image and the current end of mapped memory. To get heap space, you move the break past it.

questions.q: The current break is 0x402000. Before calling brk a second time, the program runs `mov [0x402000], rax`. What happens?
choices: The write succeeds because the data segment is global
Segmentation fault: that address is at the program break and isn't reserved yet
The kernel extends the break automatically to make room
The value is silently dropped
questions.explain: Memory at and beyond the program break isn't reserved, so the write causes a segfault.

questions.q: After brk moves the break from 0x402000 to 0x402400, `mov [0x402000], rax` succeeds and the value can be read back from 0x402000.
questions.explain: Moving the break reserved 0x402000 through 0x402400, so that address is now legal to write to. Examining it in GDB showed 1234.

questions.q: The address of the start of the heap is saved in an 8-byte variable called `buffer`. Which sequence (Intel syntax) correctly writes 1234 to the start of the heap?
choices:
mov rax, [buffer]
mov rbx, 1234
mov [rax], rbx

mov rax, [buffer]
mov rbx, 1234
mov rax, rbx

mov rbx, 1234
mov [buffer], rbx

mov rax, [buffer]
mov rbx, 1234
mov [rbx], rax
questions.explain: First load the saved address from buffer into RAX. Then use RAX as a pointer: [rax] dereferences it, so the store goes to the heap. The other choices overwrite a register, overwrite the saved pointer, or write to address 1234.

questions.q: `buffer` is the only variable in .data, at 0x402000, and holds the saved start of the heap. Later the program runs `mov [0x402000], rax` to write test data 'to the heap'. What's the bug?
choices: Nothing is wrong. 0x402000 is the start of the heap
It overwrites the saved heap-start pointer in buffer instead of writing to the heap
It causes a segfault because .data is read-only
It writes to the stack instead of the heap
questions.explain: Once .data has a variable at 0x402000, the heap no longer starts there. The hard-coded address clobbers buffer. The fix is to load the address from buffer and dereference it.

questions.category: Page alignment and the data segment
questions.q: A 1-byte variable is added to .data, and it lands at 0x402000. Where does brk(0) now report the program break?
questions.explain: The data segment now takes up one whole page, so the break, and with it the start of the heap, moves to 0x403000.

questions.category: Page alignment and the data segment
questions.q: The heap start moved from 0x402000 to 0x403000. How many bytes is the 0x1000 difference, in decimal?
questions.explain: 0x1000 = 4096 bytes, which is one page of memory.

questions.category: Page alignment and the data segment
questions.q: Why does adding a single byte to .data push the heap start back by 0x1000?
choices: The assembler pads every variable to 4096 bytes
The kernel maps memory in whole pages, so the data segment gets a full 4096-byte page
brk always reserves 4096 bytes no matter what you ask for
ASLR adds a random offset
questions.explain: You asked for one byte, but the kernel hands out a whole page anyway, so addresses stay aligned to 4096 bytes.

questions.category: Page alignment and the data segment
questions.q: You reserved 1 byte in .data but got a whole 4096-byte page. Should you use the other 4095 bytes?
choices: Yes. They're guaranteed to be yours
No. Any access to them always segfaults
Writing to them may work, but it's unreliable because you never reserved them. Reserve the space explicitly
Only if you call brk(0) first
questions.explain: Whether that extra space exists depends on the linker and toolchain. If you need the space, reserve it explicitly.

questions.category: Page alignment and the data segment
questions.q: Why do .data variables keep landing at the same address (such as 0x402000) every run in this environment?
choices: Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR) is turned off
x86-64 always loads .data at 0x402000
The brk syscall pins the data segment
GDB rewrites addresses to make them predictable
questions.explain: With ASLR turned on, which is normal on a modern system, these addresses would be random. With it off, the memory layout is the same every run.

questions.category: Page alignment and the data segment
questions.q: The main purpose of ASLR is to make programs run faster.
questions.explain: ASLR is a security feature. Randomizing the memory layout makes it harder to attack a program or run malicious code.

questions.q: To shrink the heap back later, what must the program do right after the first brk(0) call?
choices: Nothing. The kernel remembers the original break
Save the returned address (the original break) in a variable, such as an 8-byte slot in .data or .bss
Push RDI onto the stack and never pop it
Call brk with a negative size
questions.explain: Once the break moves, the original value is lost unless you saved it. It's a 64-bit address, so it needs an 8-byte (quad) variable.

questions.q: The original break is stored in `buffer`. Which sequence gives the heap back?
choices:
mov rax, 12
mov rdi, [buffer]
syscall

mov rax, 12
mov rdi, 0
syscall

mov rax, [buffer]
mov rdi, 12
syscall

mov rax, 60
mov rdi, [buffer]
syscall
questions.explain: Call brk (12 in RAX) with the original break in RDI. The kernel moves the break back and returns it in RAX. Calling brk(0) only asks for the current break, and 60 is a different syscall.

questions.q: If a program never moves the break back, its heap memory stays allocated even after the program exits.
questions.explain: The kernel takes the memory back when the program ends. Shrinking the break yourself matters only if you want to return the memory sooner.

questions.q: Moving the program break back to its original value is most like which stack operation?
choices: Pushing a return address
Resetting the stack pointer (or base pointer) after reserving space on the stack
Calling a function
Swapping RSP and RIP
questions.explain: Both reserve space by moving a boundary and release it by moving the boundary back to where it was.

questions.q: Which GDB command makes disassembly show Intel syntax instead of the default AT&T?
choices: set disassembly-flavor intel
layout intel
set syntax noprefix
.intel_syntax noprefix
questions.explain: The `.intel_syntax noprefix` directive affects only how the assembler reads your source. GDB needs its own `set disassembly-flavor intel` setting.

questions.q: What does GDB's `starti` command do?
choices: Runs the program to completion
Starts the program and stops before its very first instruction
Steps into the next function call
Restarts GDB with Intel syntax
questions.explain: starti starts the program and stops right away at the first instruction, so you can single-step from the very beginning.

questions.q: Which short GDB command executes exactly one machine instruction?
questions.explain: si (stepi) moves forward one instruction at a time.

questions.q: Which one-letter GDB command shows the contents of memory at an address (for example, to check that 1234 was written to 0x403000)?
questions.explain: The x (examine) command shows memory, for example `x 0x403000`. `print &buff` shows a symbol's address instead.

questions.q: In the build line `as break.s -o break.o && ld break.o -o break`, what does `&&` do?
choices: Runs both commands at the same time
Runs ld only if as succeeded
Runs ld only if as failed
Sends as's output into ld
questions.explain: With &&, the second command runs only if the first succeeds. If assembly fails, the chain stops.

questions.q: A build script named `b` shows 'permission denied' when you run it. Which command fixes that, giving the owner read, write, and execute permission?
choices: chmod 700 b
chmod 400 b
chown 700 b
chmod 007 b
questions.explain: 7 = rwx for the owner, and 0 = no permissions for group and others. The script also needs a correct shebang line, such as #!/bin/bash.

questions.q: Which file can hold GDB commands (such as the Intel flavor and layout settings) that run automatically every time GDB starts?
choices: .gdbinit
.bashrc
.gdb_history
gdb.conf in the current directory
questions.explain: Commands in .gdbinit run when GDB starts, so you don't have to pass them with -ex every time.

questions.q: A program makes the brk calls but never calls the exit syscall. Run outside GDB, it crashes with a segmentation fault. Why?
choices: brk always segfaults outside a debugger
Without an exit syscall, the CPU keeps executing past the end of the code
The program break was set too high
ld didn't mark the file as executable
questions.explain: A program in assembly has to end with the exit syscall. Otherwise, execution runs past the last instruction into memory that isn't valid code, which segfaults.
